questions.q: Topic 8 describes heritage tourism as "tourism as experience". Which qualities should a heritage tourism product have?
questions.explain: Topic 8: the lecture examines how to build holistic, immersive and place-based tourism products with emotional connection and narrative design.

questions.q: Which visitor segment in heritage marketing seeks deep historical context and academic accuracy?
questions.explain: Topic 9: cultural explorers want depth and accuracy; experience seekers want visuals and shareability; families want interactive learning and amenities.

questions.q: Which tactics are named in Topic 9 for flow management and de-seasonalization? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explain: Topic 9: dynamic pricing, after-hours night tours and off-season (winter) festivals balance the visitor load.

questions.q: The final lecture (Topic 15) names climate change, digitalization, inclusivity and community empowerment as key trends for heritage tourism.
questions.explain: Topic 15: these four trends are listed in the syllabus summary of the lecture on the future of heritage tourism.

questions.q: Which document (1972) links cultural and natural site protection under Outstanding Universal Value (OUV)?
questions.explain: Topic 10: Venice Charter (1964) – authenticity and integrity; UNESCO World Heritage Convention (1972) – OUV; ICOMOS Cultural Tourism Charter (1999) – sustainable visitor management.

questions.q: Listing a property on the National Register automatically stops a private owner from changing or demolishing it.
questions.explain: Topic 10: listing alone does not restrict private owner actions unless federal funding or permits are involved.

options: A tax on hotel guests in a historic district
A voluntary, binding agreement that restricts development rights in perpetuity while the property stays private
A temporary permit to hold a festival at a monument
A ban on private vehicles in a historic core
questions.explain: Topic 10: easements are voluntary and perpetual, run with the land deed, keep private ownership and give tax benefits.

questions.q: In the framework comparison (Topic 10), what is the main limitation of local zoning and design commissions?
questions.explain: Topic 10: local tools have direct binding architectural power but are vulnerable to local political pressure.

questions.q: The legal lecture gives Machu Picchu as an example of a daily visitor cap of 2,500 under UNESCO protection guidelines.
questions.explain: Topic 10: the visitor policy slide shows a 2,500 daily visitor cap at Machu Picchu.

questions.q: What is the average economic multiplier for cultural heritage investment given in Topic 11?
questions.explain: Topic 11: 1.8x–2.5x; every $1 in conservation yields up to $2.50 in indirect regional returns.

questions.q: Which of these are risks of over-commercialization of heritage (Topic 11)? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explain: Topic 11: the three risks are physical degradation, authenticity loss and economic displacement. Craft jobs are a benefit, not a risk.

questions.q: In the target revenue allocation model (Topic 11), which share goes to direct site conservation and restoration?
questions.explain: Topic 11: 40% conservation, 30% community and infrastructure fund, 20% visitor management and education, 10% administration.

questions.q: What is the last stage of the five-stage heritage event production lifecycle?
options: Legacy – site restoration and impact review
Delivery – live interpretation and visitor flow
Logistics – permits, staging and crowd routing
Research – archive audit and theme definition
questions.explain: Topic 12: Research → Co-design → Logistics → Delivery → Legacy.

questions.q: Which measures protect fragile heritage spaces during events (Topic 12)? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Drilling stage fixings into historic masonry for stability
Timed entry to respect carrying capacity
questions.explain: Topic 12: carrying capacity (timed entry), zero-trace staging (freestanding rigs, no drilling into masonry) and controlled sound and light levels.

questions.q: What was the main finding of Laurajane Smith's study (4,502 interviews in 45 museums)?
options: Visitors come mainly to buy souvenirs
Visitors come primarily to feel, not merely to learn
Visitors do not care about emotions
questions.explain: Topic 13: the study showed that visitors come primarily to feel, not merely to learn.

questions.q: Which register of emotional engagement means discomfort from confronting difficult truths?
questions.explain: Topic 13: affirmation reinforces values, empathy connects with past lives, re-evaluation is discomfort from difficult truths.
